chapter: Leaving the band, Strayhorn and reflections
title: Freddy Jenkins, the showman 'Posey'
summary: Greer describes Jenkins playing left-handed and imitating Louis's high notes, and the Prince of Wales loving him.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Now, what about Freddy Jenkins? We didn't ask you that.

Freddy? Posey? . Man, Freddy Jenkins was a master showman. He played that trumpet left-handed, he idolized Louis Armstrong. The first time he heard Louis, when he went to California to make the picture and we went out to Sebastian's Cotton Club, Louis was playing out there with Les Hite, Lionel was on the drums, Hamp was on the drums. We used to go out there, of course night like, we'd go out there. And Louis used to play this number, I forget the name of it, and hit the high notes and everybody in California would count and bet how many would hit. They'd count like one, two, and that was the highlight.
Freddy Jenkins heard that jump, he loved Louis so much he told Duke, say, I'm going to play that number. I'm

going to hit them high notes, too. So he did. Duke thought he was kidding. So he did. So he used -- I forget that (inaudible). He used that group, Duke put it in the act, played this number, pushed some stuff around.

But Freddy Jenkins, he was a picture. His left hand -- oh, he was cute. He was about the size of Billy Strayhorn, he would hit them high notes and twirl that horn someway with his left hand. Perfect showman. And the people loved him because, you know, he's tiny. They called him "Posey". He was a knockout. Prince of Wales saw him in Europe-- went crazy. Because he's small, too. Crazy. Never seen nobody like Freddy.
Didn't he have like -- he lost the fingertips on his right hand or something?
One fingertip, yeah. One or two.
Missing one or two fingers on his right hand, tips of the fingers?
Is that the reason he played with his left hand?
Yeah. He was a knockout, yeah. Posey.
